title: Ancient Coins Reveal a Wealth of Information About the Roman Republic - Nautilus
gist: Researchers from the University of São Paulo used old Roman coins as a data source to draw new economic and political insights about the last two centuries of the Roman Republic, a period marked by wars, conquest, and consolidation before Rome became an empire in 27 BCE.

themes.theme: Coinage as an economic-historical data source

insights.claim: Two researchers from the University of São Paulo in Brazil used analysis of old Roman coins to generate new insights into the final two centuries of the Roman Republic, a period defined by wars, conquest, and the consolidation of Roman hegemony over increasingly distant territories, ending with the rise of the Empire in 27 BCE.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Demonstrates coinage as a durable proxy dataset for reconstructing ancient economic and political conditions — a methodology parallel to modern uses of monetary/currency data as a macroeconomic indicator.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Two researchers from the University of São Paulo"

insights.claim: The article frames the late Roman Republic (the two centuries before 27 BCE) as a period of active territorial expansion and hegemonic consolidation, providing historical context for why coinage from that era is analytically rich.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Positions coin-based economic history as most informative during periods of geopolitical upheaval and expansion — a lens applicable to studying other historical currency regimes during conquest or empire-building.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Before it rose to imperial status"
